Thanks again for the time on Tuesday. We're finalizing our internal sizing for a Dedicated cluster and need to clarify how Redwood handles short-duration bursts vs sustained peaks. A few concrete asks from our infra team: 

- If our traffic doubles for ~6 hours (spike from nightly batch verification), how would Dedicated burst scheduling work?
- What eviction policies apply when reserved capacity is saturated and ephemeral requests arrive?
- Can we attach a simplified cost model to the burst lanes so procurement can sign off?

I'm attaching our rough demand spreadsheet (SignalWorks_Capacity_Model.xlsx) — you should be able to see the per-endpoint QPS and token distribution. Would love a short doc or checklist we can include in the SOW amendment.

Hi Olivia — thanks for the spreadsheet, that helps a lot. I've pulled together an initial sketch of how Redwood Dedicated can handle the scenarios you outlined; attaching our runbook draft (redwood_burst_runbook_v1.md) and a short cost sketch.

High level summary (TL;DR):
- Short bursts (~<8 hours): we recommend attaching a transient "shoulder slab" (ephemeral GPU pool) that can absorb the uplift. It can be billed either as a short-term usage add-on or pre-committed shoulder capacity depending on predictability.
- Eviction policy: reserved pool requests have strict priority — ephemeral jobs are preemptible and evicted first. We support weighted queues so critical endpoints (you can tag endpoints with route metadata) are preserved during pressure.
- Autoscaling behavior: the dedicated pool will scale horizontally (add instances) up to the reserved + shoulder limit. If that limit is reached, we will fall back to an agreed policy: (1) route to a cheaper quantized model variant, (2) throttle non-critical endpoints, (3) start revocation of ephemeral shoulder instances.

Practical ops knobs in the runbook:
- Headroom multiplier: choose a baseline multiplier (we usually recommend 1.2–1.5 for bursty workloads).
- Prewarm windows: predictive prewarm can spin ephemeral nodes 15–45 minutes ahead for known daily windows.
- Graceful eviction: we drain long-running KV caches first, then short-lived requests; incomplete requests can optionally be retried via a queued fallback.

I'm proposing a two-track commercial approach for procurement to consider: a) small monthly shoulder commit with usage credits, or b) pay-as-you-go ephemeral lane with an eviction SLA and priority routing defined in the SOW. Either can be modeled back into your spreadsheet — see the two tabs I added.

Next steps: Ben (cc) will add a short ops appendix (eviction semantics + SLO language) and Marissa can advise on amendment language. If that sounds right, I'll produce a redline-ready amendment targeting the 1st week of Dec.

Onboarding note: we recommend a 2-week performance soak after launch where we run synthetic spikes to validate autoscale triggers.

Thanks,

All — quick ops addendum from my side after reviewing the spreadsheet and runbook draft. I kept this short so you can drop it into the SOW appendix.

1) Eviction tiers (recommended):
   - Tier 0: Reserved customer workloads (non-preemptible) — cannot be evicted except by explicit admin action.
   - Tier 1: Tagged critical endpoints (customer-managed tags; retainable during soft pressure).
   - Tier 2: Shoulder/ephemeral lanes (preemptible after N seconds of queuing).
   - Tier 3: Public fallback (hosted models / quantized variants).

2) Credit accounting for shoulder usage: we recommend a rolling 30-day credit window. SignalWorks would get X hours per month at reduced rate, overage billed at Y. This is what procurement usually prefers since it smooths unpredictability.

3) Instrumentation hooks: add a token-level metric for 'preemptibility_score' so your SREs can tag endpoints that should survive vs be throttled automatically. We'll expose that in Console.

4) Runbook excerpt (for your ops): attach a short playbook for graceful failover — includes steps to (a) enable queued fallback, (b) escalate to Redwood on-call, (c) trigger manual shoulder carve-in.

If you're good with the above, Marissa — can you draft amendment language with the two commercial tracks Soojin suggested? I'd target the "rolling credit" option as the default unless procurement pushes back.

Cheers,
Ben
Principal Product Ops, Redwood Inference
